passage: Simran was playing a farm game on the family tablet in their Indore flat when a message popped up from a player called "SkyFriend". At first it was just tips about crops. Then: "Which school do you go to? Send a pic, I'll send you free coins." Simran's thumb hovered over the camera button. Her stomach felt funny. She put the tablet down and went to her older sister. "Kashish Didi, someone wants my school name and a photo." Kashish read the chat. "You did the right thing coming to me." Together they blocked and reported the player, and told Mummy at dinner.

qa.q: What did the player offer Simran in return for a photo?
qa.a: The player offered free coins.

qa.q: What does Simran's funny stomach feeling suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she sensed something was wrong and felt uneasy about the request.

qa.q: What did Simran do that kept her safe?
qa.a: She didn't send anything, went to her older sister, and they blocked, reported and told Mummy.

qa.q: How might Kashish feel when Simran comes to her?
qa.a: She may feel worried about the stranger but relieved and proud that Simran trusted her.

grounding: It shows a child refusing to share personal details and telling a trusted person about pressuring online contact.

passage:
"Papa, can I ask something?"
Kishore looked up from his newspaper. "Of course, Hafsa."
"Someone in the game chat says I won a prize. They want our home address. And they said don't tell your parents."
Kishore put the paper down. "Show me."
Hafsa held out the tablet, eyes down. "Am I in trouble?"
"No. You did exactly right. When someone says 'don't tell your parents', that's the biggest sign to tell us."
"So there's no prize?"
"I don't think so. Let's block them and report it together."

qa.q: What did the person in the game chat want from Hafsa?
qa.a: They wanted her home address.

qa.q: Why did Hafsa keep her eyes down and ask if she was in trouble?
qa.a: She was worried she might be blamed or punished for what happened in the chat.

qa.q: What did Kishore do that makes Hafsa likely to tell him again?
qa.a: He listened calmly, said she wasn't in trouble, praised her and helped her block and report.

qa.q: What would change if Kishore had shouted at Hafsa?
qa.a: She might hide future problems online instead of telling him, which would be less safe. 🙏

grounding: It shows a child telling a trusted adult about pressuring online contact and not sharing her address.

passage: I'm Nazia. I was twelve when it happened, and I still remember how my hands felt cold. Someone I didn't know joined a class group chat and started messaging me privately. First he said my drawings were amazing. Then he kept asking for a photo of me, again and again, and said I was being rude by saying no. I didn't reply, but I couldn't sleep. The next day I told Sabina Khala, my aunt, who's a teacher. She didn't panic. She helped me screenshot, block and report him, and told the school. I learned that saying no online is allowed, and telling someone is brave, not babyish.

qa.q: Who did Nazia tell about the messages?
qa.a: Nazia told Sabina Khala, the aunt who is a teacher.

qa.q: What does Nazia not being able to sleep suggest about how Nazia felt?
qa.a: It suggests Nazia was anxious and upset by the pressure, even though no reply was sent.

qa.q: Which choices helped Nazia most?
qa.a: Not replying, telling a trusted adult, and then screenshotting, blocking and reporting with Sabina Khala's help.

qa.q: How might Sabina Khala see Nazia telling her?
qa.a: She probably feels grateful Nazia trusted her and glad she could help calmly.

grounding: It shows a child refusing to share a photo and telling a trusted adult about pressuring online contact.

passage: Computer club note, Thursday. During free time Ira, age ten, was playing the drawing game on the lab laptop. A player she did not know began chatting: he liked her art, asked which school she went to, then asked for a photo 'just of your face'. Ira stopped drawing. She typed nothing back, closed the chat window and came straight to my desk, arms folded tight. 'Ma'am, someone is asking weird things,' she said quietly. We looked at the screen together. I praised her for keeping her school name private and for telling me at once. We blocked and reported the account. I phoned her mother after class. Tomorrow I will ask the whole club: who are your trusted adults? — Ms Pema

qa.q: Which details did the unknown player ask Ira for?
qa.a: He asked which school she went to and for a photo of her face.

qa.q: How can you tell Ira felt uneasy about the chat?
qa.a: She stopped drawing, typed nothing, closed the window and came over with her arms folded tight, saying someone was asking weird things.

qa.q: What small step could Ms Pema's club take so more children act like Ira?
qa.a: Each child could name their own trusted adults and practise the steps: don't reply, close the chat, tell an adult straight away.

qa.q: How might Ira's mother feel after the phone call?
qa.a: She might feel a jolt of worry, and then relief and pride that Ira kept her details private and told a teacher quickly.

grounding: Shows a child refusing to share personal details and telling a trusted adult about pressuring online contact.

passage: Tuesday night. Dear diary, today was strange. In the racing game there is a boy called SpeedKing who is always on my team. Today he said I was his best teammate ever and asked for my phone number so we could talk 'outside the game'. Then he wrote, 'Don't tell your parents, they won't get it.' My stomach went funny. That line made it feel wrong. I didn't send anything. I left the game and my hands were a bit shaky. I told Jahnavi didi first because she was in my room, and she took me to Mummy. Mummy wasn't angry at all. She said I did exactly right. We reported him together. I still like racing. — Akash

qa.q: What did SpeedKing ask Akash for?
qa.a: He asked for Akash's phone number so they could talk outside the game.

qa.q: Why did the message make Akash feel his stomach 'go funny'?
qa.a: The line telling him not to tell his parents made the friendly chat feel secretive and wrong, which scared him.

qa.q: What would you advise a child who gets a message like this?
qa.a: Don't reply or share anything, leave the game, and tell a trusted grown-up straight away, just like Akash did.

qa.q: What might Jahnavi have been thinking when Akash told her?
qa.a: She probably felt worried for her little brother and glad he trusted her, so she took him to Mummy at once. 🙏

grounding: Illustrates a child keeping his number private and reporting pressuring, secretive online contact to trusted adults.

passage:
In their small town near Jalna, Hrithik, eleven, was playing a car-racing game on his uncle's phone, with his friend Tanvir watching.
A message popped up from a player called SpeedKing: Which school do you go to? Send a photo in your uniform. Don't tell anyone, it's our secret.
Hrithik's stomach went tight. “Why does he want my school?”
“Don't answer,” said Tanvir. “Secrets with strangers are bad.”
Hrithik closed the chat without replying. They walked to the kitchen and showed his mother.
She read it, put the phone down and hugged him. “You did exactly right by telling me.” That evening she blocked and reported the player with his uncle, changed the game settings so strangers couldn't message, and called his class teacher to let the school know.

qa.q: What did SpeedKing ask Hrithik to send?
qa.a: A photo in his uniform.

qa.q: How did Hrithik feel when he read the message?
qa.a: He felt uneasy and worried, his stomach going tight at the stranger's questions.

qa.q: Why was showing his mother the right step?
qa.a: It ended the contact and got a trusted adult involved, who could block, report and tell the school.

qa.q: How did Hrithik's mother respond when he showed her?
qa.a: She stayed calm, hugged him, praised him for telling, and acted that same evening to block, report and inform the school.

grounding: An eleven-year-old refuses to share personal details with a stranger online and tells a trusted adult, who acts the same day.

passage:
In Osaka, Jin, ten, had been quiet all through dinner. His sister Yuki noticed he kept checking his tablet.
After dinner she sat beside him. “What's wrong?”
He showed her. In his game chat, someone had been sending him messages for three days: You're useless. Give me your password or I'll tell everyone you cheated.
“I didn't cheat,” Jin whispered. His eyes were wet.
“Come on,” said Yuki. “We're telling Papa. Now.”
Their father read the messages slowly. “Thank you for showing me, Jin. You haven't done anything wrong.”
That night they took screenshots, blocked the account, reported it to the game, and changed Jin's password together. Papa also turned off chat with strangers.

qa.q: What did the person demand from Jin?
qa.a: His password.

qa.q: How was Jin feeling about the messages?
qa.a: He felt upset and frightened, his eyes wet, especially about being falsely accused of cheating.

qa.q: What steps did Jin's family take that night, and why were they wise?
qa.a: They took screenshots, blocked and reported the account, changed the password and turned off stranger chat, which stopped the pressure and kept evidence.

qa.q: How did Yuki help her brother?
qa.a: She noticed he was quiet, asked what was wrong and made sure they told their father straight away.

grounding: A ten-year-old tells a trusted adult about pressuring online messages, and his father acts that night.

passage:
At the end of computer class, Pema, eleven, waited until the others left. “Ma'am, can I show you something?”
On her school email was a message from an unknown account: You're so pretty. Send me a photo in your uniform. Don't tell your teacher.
Pema's hands were trembling. “I didn't reply.”
Ms Tanuja sat down beside her. “Thank you for telling me, Pema. You did the right thing, and none of this is your fault.”
She stayed with Pema while they saved the message and blocked the sender. Then she walked Pema to the school's safeguarding lead, Mrs Bhutia, who called Pema's mother before the last bell. The school reported the account that afternoon.

qa.q: What did the message tell Pema not to do?
qa.a: It told her not to tell her teacher.

qa.q: How was Pema feeling when she showed Ms Tanuja?
qa.a: She felt frightened and unsettled, her hands trembling.

qa.q: What did Ms Tanuja do right after Pema told her?
qa.a: She thanked Pema, said it wasn't her fault, stayed with her, saved and blocked the message, and took her to the safeguarding lead the same day.

qa.q: How might Pema's mother feel when Mrs Bhutia calls?
qa.a: She may feel shaken, but grateful that Pema spoke up and the school acted quickly.

grounding: An eleven-year-old tells a teacher about an upsetting online message, and the school responds the same day.

Gurleen, come, sit. You're asking why I fuss about your tablet. Let me tell you about when I was eleven.
Back then, there was an internet café near our school. I used to go to a chat room about cricket. One man there was very friendly. He knew everything about cricket. After a week, he asked for my phone number and said, "Don't tell your parents, they won't understand."
That word, "don't tell," made my ears go hot. I logged off. I walked home and told my mother that same evening.
She called the café owner, who banned that account from the café computers.
That is why your Jeevan mama asks questions.

passage:
Maria, eleven, was playing an online game on her mother's phone while her mother cooked. The internet kept dropping, and her little brother Zubin kept asking for a turn.
A player called StarFox99 sent a message: "You're really good! What school do you go to? Send a photo, I'll add you to our team. Don't tell your parents, they'll ruin it."
Maria's stomach went cold. Zubin was tugging her arm. The game was about to restart.
She didn't answer. She tapped the block button, then walked straight into the kitchen. "Mama, someone asked for my school and a photo and told me to keep it secret."
Her mother turned off the stove. They reported the account together that evening, and her mother set the game so strangers couldn't message her. "You did exactly right," she said.

qa.q: What did StarFox99 ask Maria for?
qa.a: What school she goes to and a photo.

qa.q: How did Maria feel when she read the message?
qa.a: She felt uneasy and alarmed; her stomach went cold.

qa.q: Which choices kept Maria safe?
qa.a: Not answering, blocking, and telling her mother right away, who reported the account and changed the settings.

qa.q: How might Maria's mother feel when Maria tells her?
qa.a: She likely feels worried but relieved and proud that Maria told her.

grounding: Shows a child refusing to share personal details and telling a trusted adult about a pressuring online contact.

During the Diwali holidays, Tenzin, ten, joined a drawing contest on a video site. Someone commented, "Great drawing! What's your real name and city? I'll send you a prize."
Tenzin almost typed it. Then he remembered his class teacher's rule: no name, no school, no address online.
He showed his uncle Harish, who was hanging lights on the balcony. Harish read it and frowned. "Good that you showed me. Real prizes don't need your address in a comment."
They deleted the comment and reported it together that same evening. Harish changed the settings so only friends could comment.
Tenzin felt a little disappointed about the prize, and a lot safer.

passage:
It happened during the Losar holidays last winter, when I was eleven. I'm Dolma. In an online building game, a player called StarFox kept helping me. After three days, StarFox asked which school I went to and wanted a photo "to see my teammate". Then: "Don't tell your parents, they won't understand."
My stomach went strange. My friend Hafsa had once told me that grown-ups who ask kids for secrets online are a red flag.
I went straight to Amala in the kitchen and showed her the chat. She hugged me, said, "You did exactly right, my girl," and helped me block and report StarFox that same evening. Then we changed my name in the game.
I still play, but I never share where I live or what I look like.

qa.q: What did StarFox want to see?
qa.a: StarFox wanted a photo "to see my teammate".

qa.q: What was Dolma feeling when StarFox asked for secrecy?
qa.a: Dolma felt uneasy and scared, with a strange feeling in the stomach, sensing something was wrong.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Telling Amala straight away worked, because a trusted adult helped block and report the contact the same evening and nothing personal was shared.

qa.q: How might Hafsa feel if she learned her warning helped?
qa.a: Hafsa would likely feel glad and proud that what she shared helped her friend stay safe. 🤍

grounding: Shows a child refusing to share personal details online and telling a trusted adult about a pressuring contact the same day.
